# Upstream Host & Auth-Context Resolution

How the CLI decides *which host to dial* and *which login (auth context) to
authenticate as* for every upstream call. The goal is one mental model:

> An **auth context** is a login to one **core** (the identity provider /
> login server). Every upstream call resolves to some host. That host either
> **is** a core — use the active context's core directly — or it is a
> **resource server** that advertises which cores it trusts via a
> `/.well-known` blob, so the CLI picks the context whose core is trusted and
> exchanges that context's token for the resource.

There is no separate "auth system" per service. There is one identity model
(`contexts.json`, keyed on `CoreURL`) and a set of resource servers that
accept a core's JWTs.

## The pieces

| Role | Service (prod / staging) | Hit by | Trusted-core discovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core** — IdP **and** control-plane API, co-located | `entire-core` (`us.auth.entire.io`) | `org` / `repo` / `project` / `grant`, `auth *`, `login` | none needed — the host *is* the core |
| **Resource: git cluster** | `entire-server` / `entiredb` | `git-remote-entire` (clone/push) | `/.well-known/entire-cluster.json` → `core_urls` |
| **Resource: web/data API** | `entire.io` (`partial.to`) | `activity` / `search` / `trail` / `dispatch` | `/.well-known/entire-api.json` → `trusted_issuers` (audience = the host origin) |

`contexts.json` (`$ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR/contexts.json`, shared with entiredb's
CLIs) stores each login as `{Name, CoreURL, Handle, KeychainService}` plus a
`CurrentContext` pointer. `CoreURL` is the JWT `iss` — the core that minted the
token. `entire auth use <ctx>` flips `CurrentContext`.

## Resolution per call type

### Git cluster (done — `internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery`)

`ResolveContextForCluster(host)` fetches+caches the cluster's
`/.well-known/entire-cluster.json`, reads `core_urls`, then requires the
**active context** to be issued by one of them. There is no implicit
selection — see [Account selection](#account-selection) below. The token is
then exchanged for the cluster.

### Control plane (done — this slice)

The host *is* a core, so there is no discovery. `coreapi.New()` consults
`auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget()`, which mirrors `auth status`:

1. **active context** → its `CoreURL`, with a **per-context refreshing**
   bearer (`auth.NewRefreshingLoginProvider`): the token manager is keyed on
   `c.CoreURL` as issuer, so store reads and refresh/STS hit the right core,
   and an expired access token is silently re-minted from the stored refresh
   token. This is what makes `entire auth use <ctx>` actually retarget
   `org`/`repo`/`project`/`grant`.
2. **else** (no active context) → an error wrapping `ErrNotLoggedIn` with the
   `entire login` hint. There is no fallback host: a control-plane command
   without a login has no identity to act as. (At login time `entire login
   --server` chooses where to authenticate, and the resulting context's
   `CoreURL` *is* that host — so local-dev setups keep working.)

Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/auth/control_plane.go` (resolver),
`cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go` (per-context refreshing provider),
`internal/coreapi/client.go` (`New()` + `providerSource`).

### Web/data API (done)

`activity` / `search` / `trail` / `dispatch` dial `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL`
(default `entire.io`; staging `partial.to`). `entire.io` is a **resource
server** — it validates incoming JWTs against trusted issuers
(`ENTIRE_CORE_BASE_URL` + `ENTIRE_CORE_TRUSTED_ISSUERS`) and a fixed audience
(`ENTIRE_CORE_JWT_AUDIENCE`). It now **advertises** all of this at
`/.well-known/entire-api.json`, so the CLI can map the API host back to a
core/context just like a git cluster:

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://us.auth.partial.to",
  "trusted_issuers": ["https://us.auth.partial.to", "https://eu.auth.partial.to"],
  "audience": "https://partial.to",
  "jwks_uris": {"https://us.auth.partial.to": "https://us.auth.partial.to/.well-known/jwks.json"}
}
```

The CLI reads **only `trusted_issuers`** — exactly the way the git path reads a
cluster's `core_urls`. `issuer`, `audience`, and `jwks_uris` are advertised but
ignored on decode (see the audience note below).

> **Audience = the data host origin.** entire.io's `ENTIRE_CORE_JWT_AUDIENCE` is
> `https://entire.io` (prod) / `https://partial.to` (staging) — the data host's
> own base URI, on both environments. The token manager already defaults the RFC
> 8693 audience to the resource origin it's exchanging for, so dialing
> `https://entire.io` produces `aud = https://entire.io` with no special
> handling. The CLI therefore **derives** the audience from the host it's already
> dialing rather than reading the advertised `audience` field. (This trades away
> the "server changes audience without a CLI release" flexibility — acceptable
> because `aud == base URI` is a hard requirement on both environments.)

Because the only field the CLI consumes is the trusted-issuer list — which *is*
a set of core URLs — the data-API discovery cache is literally the git cluster's
cores cache (`ClusterCoresCache`), in a separate file (`api_discovery.json`).

Resolution (`auth.ResolveDataAPIToken`):

1. Resolve the API host's trusted issuers: `api_discovery.json` when fresh, else
   a live `/.well-known/entire-api.json` fetch (TLS-authenticated — it's a trust
   root; redirects refused), cached with a 24h TTL and stale-fallback on a failed
   re-fetch. Same `resolveClusterCores` shape the git path uses.
2. Require the **active context** with the same semantics as the git path: it is
   used when its `CoreURL` is among the trusted issuers, and anything else is an
   error. So `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL=https://partial.to entire activity` needs
   `entire auth use staging` first — the target host never selects the identity
   for you.
3. Exchange that context's login JWT at **its** core for the data host origin
   (`auth.NewRefreshingResourceProvider`, keyed on `c.CoreURL` like the
   control-plane provider; the token manager sets `aud` = that origin).
4. **No fallback**: a host that doesn't advertise discovery (404 / unreachable /
   503 / malformed) with no cache entry is an error naming the host — without
   the well-known we can't know which login servers it trusts. A *reachable*
   host whose context selection fails surfaces that error — the user must log
   in or pick one. (A transient outage with a warm cache uses the stale entry.)

The selection rule differs from the control plane (where the active context is
*always* used because there's no host to match): here a host **is** matched, so
the active context is used only when the host trusts its core.

Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/auth/data_api.go` (`ResolveDataAPIToken`),
`cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go` (`NewRefreshingResourceProvider`),
`internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery/api_discovery.go` (`DiscoverAPI`,
`ResolveContextForAPI`, sharing `requireActiveContext` *and* the cores cache with
the cluster path), `internal/entireclient/discovery/cluster_cores.go`
(`LoadAPICores`/`ModifyAPICores`). Seams:
`NewAuthenticatedAPIClient` (activity/trail/search-completion),
`dispatch/mode_local.go` `lookupResourceToken` (dispatch),
`search_cmd.go` `resolveSearchToken` (search).

## Account selection

One rule, everywhere a host is matched — git clusters, the data API,
cluster-addressed control-plane commands, and entire-api cell routing
(`auth/cell_data_api.go`'s `resolveStoredCellSubject`): **the active context is
the identity, or the command fails.** `entire auth use <ctx>` is the only lever;
`/.well-known` decides only whether that identity is *accepted*, never which one
is *chosen*.

Two implicit tiers used to sit underneath — "the sole eligible context", and an
ambiguity error when several were eligible. Both are gone. They made the acting
identity depend on what else happened to be stored, so adding a second login
could silently change which account a command ran as, and the same command could
act as different identities on two machines. For "whose credentials is this
running under?", a predictable error beats a convenient guess.

Multiple saved logins are still fully supported — `auth contexts`, `auth use`,
and `logout --all-contexts` are unchanged. What changed is that switching is
always explicit.

Because "not logged in" is actively misleading for a user who *is* logged in,
just to another federation, the error distinguishes what the user can do about
it. Two independent facts pick the message
(`clusterdiscovery.renderUnusableActiveContext`): whether an active context
exists, and whether any saved login is eligible.

| Active context | A saved login is eligible | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| yes | yes | names the active login, lists the eligible ones (sorted), points at `entire auth use` |
| yes | no | names the active login, adds "no other saved login does either", then the trusted servers and `entire login --server <url>` |
| no | yes | "no active auth context for …", lists the eligible ones, points at `entire auth use` |
| no | no | the login hint, plus the trusted servers and `entire login --server <url>` |

The two no-active-context rows must not use the "does not accept your active
login" phrasing — there is no active login to reject, and a dangling
`current_context` lands there.

The advertised servers are named whenever no saved login fits, because they are
then the only actionable detail: bare `entire login` re-authenticates against the
default server, which for a resource in another federation reproduces the same
failure.

Key file: `internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery/resolve.go`
(`requireActiveContext` — the single home for this policy, plus
`contextEligible`, the one eligibility predicate shared by the accept decision
and the candidate list).

content.text:
Done. Both mechanisms, on `soph/explicit-login-selection`. `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean, `mise run test:ci` green (56 + 4 canary).

## What went in

**`contexts.File.Active()` — one owner for "which identity acts."** Precedence: `--context` → `$ENTIRE_CONTEXT` → `current_context`. This had to come first: seven separate sites resolved the active context, and overriding only some would have had `logout` revoking one identity's session server-side while deleting a different one's credentials locally. All of them now route through `Active()`, so `auth status` reports the override, `auth contexts` marks it, and `logout --context staging` revokes and removes the login it named.

**Both mechanisms, because they reach different entry points.** The flag can't reach git at all — git spawns `git-remote-entire` itself, so `ENTIRE_CONTEXT=staging git push` is the only way to scope a git operation. The env var also survives into hooks and subprocesses, which is what makes a whole shell scopable. That asymmetry is why "both" was the right instinct, not just belt-and-braces.

**An unknown name is a hard error, never a fall-through.** `contexts.UnknownContextError`, raised *before* any trust check — "that context doesn't exist" and "that context isn't trusted here" are different mistakes, and falling back to `current_context` would run the command as the wrong account and succeed while doing it.

**Errors blame the right thing.** If the identity came from `--context`, telling you to run `auth use` sends you to change something the flag would keep overriding. So the remedy tracks the source: `the login selected by --context "staging"` → "Name one with `--context <context>`", versus `your active login` → "Switch with `entire auth use`".

## Two defects only the real binary surfaced

Worth noting because unit tests were green through both:

- **Flag help rendered as `--context entire auth contexts`.** pflag treats the first back-quoted span in a usage string as the *value placeholder*, so my `` `entire auth contexts` `` got hijacked. Now back-quotes `name` deliberately → `--context name`.
- **`load contexts: --context selected login context "typo"…`** — `resolveStatusTarget` wraps every error as a load failure, which described the wrong problem. Now passes `UnknownContextError` through unwrapped.

I also avoided a trap: root's `PersistentPreRun` would have been the obvious wiring, but Cobra runs only the *closest* one in the chain, and `agent_group.go` plus the per-agent hooks commands define their own — so it would have been silently skipped for exactly the subtrees that inherited the flag. Binding through a `pflag.Value` applies it at parse time instead, with no ordering to get wrong.

Verified on the built binary: `--context staging auth contexts` marks staging active, `current_context` in `contexts.json` stays `prod` — the override doesn't persist, which is the entire point.

## Where this leaves the three-way comparison

The adversarial review's sharpest finding against my own branch was that I'd replaced a *scoped, residue-free* identity choice with a *global, sticky* one — and that for the staging/prod flow this could be worse than `main`'s auto-selection, which at least left nothing behind. That's now closed: the one-off case is a flag or an env var, and `auth use` is back to being what it should be, a way to change your default rather than the only way to do a cross-federation operation.

Two things I'd still flag as open, neither introduced here:

- **The data-API path has no `ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypass** (`ResolveDataAPIToken` never consults it), unlike git and the control plane. So CI-shaped use of `activity`/`search`/`dispatch` requires a stored login. Pre-existing asymmetry, but it's the path with the least escape hatch.
- **Nobody has measured whether auto-selection ever misfired**, or how many installs hold >1 context. Two queries would turn the B-vs-C argument from taste into evidence.

Still uncommitted — 622 insertions across 16 files plus 3 new ones, for you to read. Want me to commit and open it as a PR next to #1978?

83		}

86		if err != nil {

88		}
89	
90		selected, err := requireActiveContext(f, "cluster "+clusterHost, entry.CoreURLs, debugf)
91		if err != nil {

93		}

95			Context:              selected,
96			JurisdictionAudience: entry.JurisdictionAudience,
97			JurisdictionCoreURL:  entry.JurisdictionCoreURL,
98		}, nil

102	// control-plane core URLs that front clusterHost plus its advertised
103	// jurisdiction audience/core — using the same cache-then-/.well-known
104	// discovery as ResolveContextForCluster (see resolveClusterCores). Exported

1	# Upstream Host & Auth-Context Resolution
2	
3	How the CLI decides *which host to dial* and *which login (auth context) to
4	authenticate as* for every upstream call. The goal is one mental model:
5	
6	> An **auth context** is a login to one **core** (the identity provider /
7	> login server). Every upstream call resolves to some host. That host either
8	> **is** a core — use the active context's core directly — or it is a
9	> **resource server** that advertises which cores it trusts via a
10	> `/.well-known` blob, so the CLI picks the context whose core is trusted and
11	> exchanges that context's token for the resource.
12	
13	There is no separate "auth system" per service. There is one identity model
14	(`contexts.json`, keyed on `CoreURL`) and a set of resource servers that
15	accept a core's JWTs.
16	
17	## The pieces
18	
19	| Role | Service (prod / staging) | Hit by | Trusted-core discovery |
20	|---|---|---|---|
21	| **Core** — IdP **and** control-plane API, co-located | `entire-core` (`us.auth.entire.io`) | `org` / `repo` / `project` / `grant`, `auth *`, `login` | none needed — the host *is* the core |
22	| **Resource: git cluster** | `entire-server` / `entiredb` | `git-remote-entire` (clone/push) | `/.well-known/entire-cluster.json` → `core_urls` |
23	| **Resource: web/data API** | `entire.io` (`partial.to`) | `activity` / `search` / `trail` / `dispatch` | `/.well-known/entire-api.json` → `trusted_issuers` (audience = the host origin) |
24	
25	`contexts.json` (`$ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR/contexts.json`, shared with entiredb's
26	CLIs) stores each login as `{Name, CoreURL, Handle, KeychainService}` plus a
27	`CurrentContext` pointer. `CoreURL` is the JWT `iss` — the core that minted the
28	token. `entire auth use <ctx>` flips `CurrentContext`.
29	
30	## Resolution per call type
31	
32	### Git cluster (done — `internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery`)
33	
34	`ResolveContextForCluster(host)` fetches+caches the cluster's
35	`/.well-known/entire-cluster.json`, reads `core_urls`, then requires the
36	**active context** to be issued by one of them. There is no implicit
37	selection — see [Account selection](#account-selection) below. The token is
38	then exchanged for the cluster.
39	
40	### Control plane (done — this slice)
41	
42	The host *is* a core, so there is no discovery. `coreapi.New()` consults
43	`auth.ResolveControlPlaneTarget()`, which mirrors `auth status`:
44	
45	1. **active context** → its `CoreURL`, with a **per-context refreshing**
46	   bearer (`auth.NewRefreshingLoginProvider`): the token manager is keyed on
47	   `c.CoreURL` as issuer, so store reads and refresh/STS hit the right core,
48	   and an expired access token is silently re-minted from the stored refresh
49	   token. This is what makes `entire auth use <ctx>` actually retarget
50	   `org`/`repo`/`project`/`grant`.
51	2. **else** (no active context) → an error wrapping `ErrNotLoggedIn` with the
52	   `entire login` hint. There is no fallback host: a control-plane command
53	   without a login has no identity to act as. (At login time `entire login
54	   --server` chooses where to authenticate, and the resulting context's
55	   `CoreURL` *is* that host — so local-dev setups keep working.)
56	
57	Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/auth/control_plane.go` (resolver),
58	`cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go` (per-context refreshing provider),
59	`internal/coreapi/client.go` (`New()` + `providerSource`).
60	
61	### Web/data API (done)
62	
63	`activity` / `search` / `trail` / `dispatch` dial `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL`
64	(default `entire.io`; staging `partial.to`). `entire.io` is a **resource
65	server** — it validates incoming JWTs against trusted issuers
66	(`ENTIRE_CORE_BASE_URL` + `ENTIRE_CORE_TRUSTED_ISSUERS`) and a fixed audience
67	(`ENTIRE_CORE_JWT_AUDIENCE`). It now **advertises** all of this at
68	`/.well-known/entire-api.json`, so the CLI can map the API host back to a
69	core/context just like a git cluster:
70	
71	```json
72	{
73	  "issuer": "https://us.auth.partial.to",
74	  "trusted_issuers": ["https://us.auth.partial.to", "https://eu.auth.partial.to"],
75	  "audience": "https://partial.to",
76	  "jwks_uris": {"https://us.auth.partial.to": "https://us.auth.partial.to/.well-known/jwks.json"}
77	}
78	```
79	
80	The CLI reads **only `trusted_issuers`** — exactly the way the git path reads a
81	cluster's `core_urls`. `issuer`, `audience`, and `jwks_uris` are advertised but
82	ignored on decode (see the audience note below).
83	
84	> **Audience = the data host origin.** entire.io's `ENTIRE_CORE_JWT_AUDIENCE` is
85	> `https://entire.io` (prod) / `https://partial.to` (staging) — the data host's
86	> own base URI, on both environments. The token manager already defaults the RFC
87	> 8693 audience to the resource origin it's exchanging for, so dialing
88	> `https://entire.io` produces `aud = https://entire.io` with no special
89	> handling. The CLI therefore **derives** the audience from the host it's already
90	> dialing rather than reading the advertised `audience` field. (This trades away
91	> the "server changes audience without a CLI release" flexibility — acceptable
92	> because `aud == base URI` is a hard requirement on both environments.)
93	
94	Because the only field the CLI consumes is the trusted-issuer list — which *is*
95	a set of core URLs — the data-API discovery cache is literally the git cluster's
96	cores cache (`ClusterCoresCache`), in a separate file (`api_discovery.json`).
97	
98	Resolution (`auth.ResolveDataAPIToken`):
99	
100	1. Resolve the API host's trusted issuers: `api_discovery.json` when fresh, else
101	   a live `/.well-known/entire-api.json` fetch (TLS-authenticated — it's a trust
102	   root; redirects refused), cached with a 24h TTL and stale-fallback on a failed
103	   re-fetch. Same `resolveClusterCores` shape the git path uses.
104	2. Require the **active context** with the same semantics as the git path: it is
105	   used when its `CoreURL` is among the trusted issuers, and anything else is an
106	   error. So `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL=https://partial.to entire activity` needs
107	   `entire auth use staging` first — the target host never selects the identity
108	   for you.
109	3. Exchange that context's login JWT at **its** core for the data host origin
110	   (`auth.NewRefreshingResourceProvider`, keyed on `c.CoreURL` like the
111	   control-plane provider; the token manager sets `aud` = that origin).
112	4. **No fallback**: a host that doesn't advertise discovery (404 / unreachable /
113	   503 / malformed) with no cache entry is an error naming the host — without
114	   the well-known we can't know which login servers it trusts. A *reachable*
115	   host whose context selection fails surfaces that error — the user must log
116	   in or pick one. (A transient outage with a warm cache uses the stale entry.)
117	
118	The selection rule differs from the control plane (where the active context is
119	*always* used because there's no host to match): here a host **is** matched, so
120	the active context is used only when the host trusts its core.
121	
122	Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/auth/data_api.go` (`ResolveDataAPIToken`),
123	`cmd/entire/cli/auth/refresh.go` (`NewRefreshingResourceProvider`),
124	`internal/entireclient/clusterdiscovery/api_discovery.go` (`DiscoverAPI`,
125	`ResolveContextForAPI`, sharing `requireActiveContext` *and* the cores cache with
126	the cluster path), `internal/entireclient/discovery/cluster_cores.go`
127	(`LoadAPICores`/`ModifyAPICores`). Seams:
128	`NewAuthenticatedAPIClient` (activity/trail/search-completion),
129	`dispatch/mode_local.go` `lookupResourceToken` (dispatch),
130	`search_cmd.go` `resolveSearchToken` (search).
131	
132	## Account selection
133	
134	One rule, everywhere a host is matched — git clusters, the data API,
135	cluster-addressed control-plane commands, and entire-api cell routing
136	(`auth/cell_data_api.go`'s `resolveStoredCellSubject`): **the active context is
137	the identity, or the command fails.** `entire auth use <ctx>` is the only lever;
138	`/.well-known` decides only whether that identity is *accepted*, never which one
139	is *chosen*.
140

git commit -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(auth): require the active context, dropping implicit login selection

Account selection had three tiers: the active context when the resource
trusted its core, else "the sole eligible context", else an ambiguity
error. The two implicit tiers are removed — the active context is the
identity, or the command fails.

The tiers made the acting identity depend on what *else* happened to be
stored. Adding a second login could silently change which account an
existing command ran as, and the same command could act as different
identities on two machines. Concretely: log into prod as alice, add a
staging login as admin for one task, and `git push` to a staging-fronted
cluster would authenticate as admin — an elevated account, with the
server-side audit trail recording it, and nothing in the output saying
so. For "whose credentials is this running under?", a predictable error
beats a convenient guess.

Multiple saved logins remain fully supported; `auth contexts`, `auth use`,
and `logout --all-contexts` are unchanged. What changes is that switching
is explicit.

Because "not logged in" is actively misleading for someone who IS logged
in, just to another federation, the failure now distinguishes what the
user can do about it: name the saved logins that would work and point at
`auth use`, or name the servers the resource trusts and point at
`entire login --server <url>`. That cashes in renderLoginHint's dead
`_ []string` parameter and its "display coreURLs at a later stage" TODO —
bare `entire login` re-authenticates against the default server, which
for a resource in another federation reproduces the very failure being
reported.

selectContext is renamed requireActiveContext: it validates, it no longer
selects, and its old doc spent thirteen lines saying so.

Also fixes a latent inconsistency: eligibility was answered by two
different mechanisms in one function — contextEligible for the accept
decision and ContextsForIssuer for the candidate list — which disagreed
on blank CoreURL and on whitespace. They produced "does not accept your
active login \"blank\". These saved logins can authenticate it: blank",
telling the user to switch to the login they were already on. Both paths
now share one predicate and one URL normaliser.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

63	// control-plane command should dial — one whose subject is a mirror on a

65	// rather than the caller's own account.

70	// prod entire.io cluster). We discover the cluster's trusted cores from its

feat(auth): select a login per invocation with --context and ENTIRE_CONTEXT

Requiring the active context made every cross-federation operation go
through `entire auth use`, which is persistent and machine-wide: it
retargets the identity for every shell, worktree, and background git hook
until switched back. That is a poor trade for a one-off. It is also worse
than the implicit tier it replaced in one respect — the old fallback was
scoped to a single command and left no residue, where a forgotten
`auth use` silently retargets the next `git push`.

So add a per-invocation selection. Precedence is `--context`, then
$ENTIRE_CONTEXT, then the stored current_context.

Both mechanisms are needed because they reach different entry points. A
flag cannot reach git at all: git invokes git-remote-entire itself, so
`ENTIRE_CONTEXT=staging git push` is the only way to scope a git
operation. The env var also survives into hooks and subprocesses, which
is what makes a whole shell scopable.

Resolution moves into one owner, contexts.File.Active. Seven sites
resolved the active context independently, and overriding only some would
have had `logout` revoking one identity's session server-side while
deleting another's credentials locally. Routing them all through Active
also means the selection is coherent everywhere: `auth status` reports it,
`auth contexts` marks it, `logout` revokes and removes that login.

An override naming no saved context is a hard error
(contexts.UnknownContextError), never a fall-through to current_context —
running as an identity other than the one asked for would succeed
silently as the wrong account. It is reported before any trust check,
because "that context doesn't exist" and "that context isn't trusted
here" are different mistakes. Trust failures likewise name their source:
an identity that came from --context is fixed by changing that argument,
not by `auth use`, which the flag would keep overriding.

The flag binds through a pflag.Value rather than a PersistentPreRun:
Cobra runs only the closest PersistentPreRun in the chain, and the agent
and hooks subtrees define their own, so a root hook would be skipped for
exactly the commands that inherited the flag.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

gh pr create --base main --head soph/explicit-login-selection \

  --body-file - <<'EOF'
An alternative to #1978. Same diagnosis — implicit login selection is a footgun — but it drops **only the auto-selection**, and keeps multiple saved logins.

## The problem both PRs are solving

Account selection had three tiers: the active context when the resource trusted its core, else *"the sole eligible context"*, else an ambiguity error. The implicit tiers made the acting identity depend on what **else** happened to be stored.

Concretely: log into prod as `alice`, add a staging login as `admin` for one task, and `git push` to a staging-fronted cluster authenticates as `admin` — an elevated account you never selected for that operation, with the server-side audit trail recording it, and nothing in the output saying so. Adding a login could change what an existing command did, and the same command could act as different identities on two machines.

## What this does differently from #1978

#1978 bundles three separable decisions: (1) drop auto-selection, (2) drop multi-login, (3) move metadata into the keychain. None implies the next, and the confusion is evidence for (1) — the cheapest of the three.

This PR does (1) only. `auth contexts`, `auth use`, `logout --all-contexts`, and `contexts.json` are unchanged, so no migration, no downgrade cliff, and dual-account workflows (personal + elevated, staging + prod) keep working.

## Two commits

**1. `refactor(auth)` — require the active context.** `selectContext` becomes `requireActiveContext`: it validates, it no longer selects. Failures now distinguish what you can *do* about it, because a wrong remedy is a dead end and "not logged in" is actively misleading for someone who is logged in, just to another federation:

```
API host partial.to does not accept your active login "me@prod" (https://us.auth.entire.io).
These saved logins can authenticate it: me@staging
Switch with `entire auth use <context>`, then re-run your command.
```
```
cluster aws-eu-central-1.entire.io does not accept your active login "staging" (https://eu.auth.partial.to), and no other saved login does either.
It trusts these login servers: https://eu.auth.entire.io
Log in with `entire login --server <url>`, then re-run your command.
```

That second one cashes in `renderLoginHint`'s dead `_ []string` parameter and its *"display coreURLs at a later stage"* TODO. Naming the servers is the only actionable part — bare `entire login` re-authenticates against the default server and reproduces the same failure.

This commit also fixes a latent inconsistency: eligibility was answered by two different mechanisms in one function (`contextEligible` for the accept decision, `ContextsForIssuer` for the candidate list), which disagreed on blank `CoreURL` and on whitespace. They produced `does not accept your active login "blank". These saved logins can authenticate it: blank` — telling you to switch to the login you were already on. Both paths now share one predicate and one URL normaliser.

**2. `feat(auth)` — `--context` and `ENTIRE_CONTEXT`.** Requiring the active context sends every cross-federation operation through `auth use`, which is persistent and machine-wide. That's a bad trade for a one-off, and in one respect worse than the tier it replaced: the old fallback was scoped to a single command and left no residue, where a forgotten `auth use` silently retargets your next `git push`.

```sh
entire --context staging activity     # one command
ENTIRE_CONTEXT=staging git push       # one git operation
entire auth use staging               # your default, when you mean it
```

Both are needed because they reach different entry points — **git invokes `git-remote-entire` itself, so a flag can never reach a git operation.**

Resolution moves into one owner, `contexts.File.Active`. Seven sites resolved the active context independently; overriding only some would have had `logout` revoking one identity's session server-side while deleting another's credentials locally.

## Notes for review

- An override naming no saved context is a **hard error**, reported before any trust check. "That context doesn't exist" and "that context isn't trusted here" are different mistakes, and falling through to `current_context` would succeed as the wrong account.
- Trust failures name their source: an identity from `--context` is fixed by changing that argument, not by `auth use`, which the flag would keep overriding.
- `--context` binds through a `pflag.Value`, not a `PersistentPreRun` — Cobra runs only the closest one in the chain, and the agent and hooks subtrees define their own, so a root hook would be silently skipped for exactly the commands that inherited the flag.
- **Behaviour change worth a decision:** `ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL=https://partial.to entire activity` no longer silently picks your staging login. It now needs `--context staging` (or `ENTIRE_CONTEXT`). That was auto-selection wearing a feature's clothes — an env var quietly changing which account a command ran as — so removing it is the point, but it is a documented workflow changing shape.
- Each commit builds and passes tests on its own.

## Out of scope, surfaced while working

- The **data-API path has no `ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypass** (`ResolveDataAPIToken` never consults it), unlike git and the control plane. Pre-existing, but it is the path with the least escape hatch.
- The repo has **four hand-rolled issuer comparisons** (`contexts.trimURL`, `auth.sameIssuer`, `coreTrusted`, `contextEligible`). This unifies the two inside `clusterdiscovery`; consolidating the rest means touching `git-remote-entire` and `auth`.
- **Nobody has measured** whether auto-selection ever misfired, or how many installs hold >1 context. Two telemetry queries would turn the #1978-vs-this argument from taste into evidence.
- `CLAUDE.md` claims *"Normal lint includes dupl at threshold 75"*, but `dupl` isn't in `.golangci.yaml`'s `enable:` list — only `mise run dup` runs it. Stale, unrelated to this work.

## Verification

`mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean (0 issues). `mise run test:ci` green — unit, integration, and both canary agents (56 + 4). Behaviour also checked against the built binary: `--context staging auth contexts` marks staging active while `current_context` in `contexts.json` stays `prod`, confirming the override does not persist.

Two commits, split so each is separately reviewable — which matters here, because the first is the contentious policy change and the second is the mitigation that makes it safe:

| `8351e0f4a` | `refactor(auth): require the active context, dropping implicit login selection` |
| `02f0a7c24` | `feat(auth): select a login per invocation with --context and ENTIRE_CONTEXT` |

946 insertions / 170 deletions across 19 files.

**Each commit stands alone.** The two changes touched seven of the same files, and `git add -p` isn't available in this environment, so I reconstructed commit 1's intermediate state by hand rather than shipping a commit that wouldn't build. Then verified it properly: checked `8351e0f4a` out into a throwaway worktree and ran `go build ./...` plus the `entireclient` and `auth` test packages against it in isolation. I also diffed the restored commit-2 tree against a saved copy of the reviewed state to confirm the round-trip didn't silently drop anything — the shared files match byte-for-byte, and the three new files I retyped are covered by the full `test:ci` pass.

Both messages explain *why* rather than *what* — commit 1 leads with the concrete silent-elevation scenario (prod as `alice`, staging as `admin`, `git push` authenticating as the elevated account with the audit trail recording it), commit 2 leads with the reason the override is needed at all, including that it partly inverts commit 1's own trade-off.

The PR body frames this explicitly as an alternative to #1978, makes the "#1978 bundles three separable decisions" argument, and carries forward the four things worth knowing that came out of the review but are out of scope: the missing `ENTIRE_TOKEN` bypass on the data-API path, the four remaining issuer-comparison implementations, the absence of any measurement to settle #1978-vs-this empirically, and the stale `dupl` claim in `CLAUDE.md`.

Compared to **#1978**: both remove the implicit auto-selection that could silently authenticate you as an account you never picked, but #1978 also deletes multi-login entirely (keychain migration, one login, `auth contexts`/`auth use`/`--all-contexts` gone), while mine keeps every saved login and `contexts.json` untouched — no migration, no downgrade cliff, staging+prod and personal+admin still work.

The trade is that mine makes switching explicit, so it adds `--context` and `ENTIRE_CONTEXT` for one-off cross-federation commands (a flag can't reach `git push`, hence both), plus errors that name which saved login or which login server would actually work instead of #1978's dead-end "not logged in" when you are in fact logged in.

content.text:
Your question found a bug. Answering both, then what I did about it.

## `logout`

Unchanged in shape from `main` — three flags, same flow: resolve the target → revoke server-side → delete local credentials → promote the next saved login.

```
entire logout                    # revoke this session, remove the acting login
entire logout --everywhere       # revoke every session on that login server (all devices)
entire logout --all-contexts     # drain every saved login, each against its own core
```

What's new is that `--context`/`ENTIRE_CONTEXT` retarget it, which gives you something `main` couldn't do — log out of a *specific non-active* login:

| command (active = staging) | result |
|---|---|
| `entire logout` | removes staging, promotes prod → `current=prod` |
| `entire logout --context staging` | same — removes staging, promotes prod |
| `entire logout --context prod` | removes prod, leaves `current=staging` |

Revocation and local deletion resolve through the same `Active()`, which is why I moved resolution into one owner: otherwise `--context staging` would revoke staging's session server-side while deleting prod's credentials locally.

**The bug your question surfaced:** row 2 originally produced `current=None` — same target as row 1, different end state, purely because you named it. `promoteNextLogin` asked for the *acting* identity, which by then resolved the still-set override to the context logout had just deleted; `Active()` returned `UnknownContextError`, and since promotion is best-effort it swallowed the error and silently skipped. You'd end up with saved logins and no active one.

Fixed in `400880cf3`: `Contexts()` answers "which identity is acting" (for status and revocation), the new `StoredContexts()` answers "what is persisted" (for promotion) and ignores the override. Regression test pins both. Table above is the verified post-fix behaviour.

## `login` while already logged in

**Untouched by my branch** — identical to `main`. It keys on the token's `iss` + handle claims:

- **Same identity** (same core, same handle) → updates that context in place, keeps its name, carries `JurisdictionAudiences` over, makes it active. Effectively a token refresh.
- **New identity on the same core** → a *new* context named `handle@host` (numeric suffix if that's taken too), which becomes active. Your old login stays saved and usable.
- **Different core** (`login --server …`) → new context named after that host, becomes active.

So on this branch logging in never destroys an existing login — worth contrasting with **#1978**, where `RecordLogin` calls `deleteContextKeychain` on the previous login, so its credentials are gone rather than parked, and switching back means another browser flow.

Two rough edges I'd flag rather than leave you to find:

- `--context` is accepted on `login` but does nothing (it's a root persistent flag, and login creates rather than selects). Harmless but confusable; a validation error would be kinder.
- Context names are machine-generated (`me@core.entire.io`), so `auth use` and `--context` take names you didn't choose. `main` has the same wart — there's no `login --name`.

PR #1982 is now three commits. I used a follow-up commit rather than amending so nothing force-pushes over a public branch; say the word if you'd rather I squash it into the `feat` commit.

content.text:
Essentially yes — and this cuts against the branch I just built, so let me be straight about it.

**Only one code path creates a context at all:** `RecordLoginContext`, called from exactly one place, `persistLogin` in `login.go`. Nothing else — not `enable`, not `repo clone`, not the setup flow — ever writes one. So contexts come only from `entire login`.

A second context requires a different `(coreURL, handle)` pair, where `coreURL` is the token's signed `iss` claim. That leaves exactly two reachable routes:

1. **`entire login --server <url>`** — visible, not hidden, but its own help says *"rarely needed; the default serves all standard accounts."* The product describes this as an edge case in its own flag text.
2. **`entire login` twice, authenticating as different accounts on the same server** — no flags. `pickContextName` finds no `(core, handle)` match, the bare host name is taken, so you get a second context named `admin@us.auth.entire.io`.

And the env route is deliberately closed: `ENTIRE_AUTH_BASE_URL` is retired and **hard-fails every command** when set, pointing you at `--server`. That's the product actively narrowing multi-core usage, not accommodating it.

So: a single-account user on the default server will only ever have one context — re-login updates it in place. Route 2 needs no flags but does need you to deliberately authenticate as someone else (the browser flow gives you whoever you already are). Nothing in the happy path produces a second login by accident.

**What that does to the comparison.** If multi-login is empty in practice, #1978's headline cost — capability loss — is close to zero, and my `--context` work is solving a problem nobody has. The argument then stops being "does this break multi-federation users" and becomes narrower and more tractable:

- **Both** PRs remove auto-selection, which is worth doing in either world — that's the actual defect, and it's cheap.
- What's left of #1978's cost is the *migration*: one-way `contexts.json` deletion, downgrade reads as logged out, keychain opacity for debugging, un-upgraded `entiredb`, and the three concrete bugs I filed (the dead-end error, orphaned credentials on the empty-`current_context` path, the `sha256(path-string)` aliasing). All fixable.
- What's left of #1982's cost is carrying a capability nobody exercises.

Two caveats before you conclude. Route 2 covers personal-plus-work and human-plus-service-account, which are plausible without anything exotic. And the people most likely to use `--server` are your own team on `partial.to` — so "nobody has this" may be false precisely for the engineers shipping the change.

This is now a very answerable question rather than a matter of taste: count installs whose `contexts.json` has more than one entry. If that number is ~0, I'd take #1978's direction with my three findings fixed, and drop #1982's commit 2 as unnecessary — commit 1 is the part that matters either way. Want me to work out how to measure it?

fix(auth): skip nil stored contexts instead of dereferencing them

A hand-edited or truncated contexts.json can hold `{"contexts":[null]}` —
the same trust boundary deleteContextKeychain's blank-audience guard
already contemplates. Every reader of f.Contexts now skips such an entry.

This was widened by the eligibleContexts rewrite two commits ago. The old
shape iterated coreURLs on the outside, so an empty core list dereferenced
nothing at all; the new one walks every stored entry and dereferences each
immediately. contexts.File.Find had the same gap, and Active() resolves
through it, so a nil entry panicked before eligibility was even consulted.
Names(), added in the same commit, did guard — the inconsistency is what
gave it away.

It matters because the failure path runs inside git-remote-entire during
`git push`, where a stack trace is the worst outcome available.

ContextsForIssuer gets the same guard so all three readers of f.Contexts
agree, rather than leaving one of them as the odd one out.

Reported by Copilot on #1982.
